findings.message: The ENTROPY expression calls `.otherwise()` on the result of `F.sum(...)` rather than on a `F.when(...)`, so every generated script with an ENTROPY metric fails at runtime when the expression is built. `_distributional_agg_expr` returns `F.sum(F.when({cv} > 0, -{p} * F.log({p}))).otherwise(F.lit(0.0))`. The `.otherwise` is attached to the Column that `F.sum` returns. Spark's `Column.otherwise` raises IllegalArgumentException ("otherwise() can only be applied on a Column previously generated by when() function") on any other Column. The default test fixture `_pipeline_full` uses `DistributionalMetric.ENTROPY`, so the full script breaks inside `build_layer2b`. The tests only run `ast.parse`, so they pass.

Requesting ENTROPY produces an invalid Spark expression and prevents the pipeline from completing. The ENTROPY branch emits F.sum(F.when(...)).otherwise(F.lit(0.0)); otherwise is applied to the aggregate rather than the when expression. Spark permits otherwise only on a Column produced by when, so executing the generated Layer 2B code fails.

MODE returns an arbitrary category (whichever row `F.first` meets first) instead of the category with the largest share, so the MODE feature column holds wrong values. `if metric == DistributionalMetric.MODE: return f'F.first(F.col("{cat_col}"), ignorenulls=True).alias(...)'`. It runs inside `_shares_{i}.groupBy(id, time).agg(...)` with no ordering by `{cat}_..._cat_val`. `first()` inside a groupBy aggregate is non-deterministic and ignores the share column entirely. Any distributional categorical configured with MODE (see `_pipeline_all_metrics`) produces this column.

MODE returns an arbitrary category instead of the category with the greatest aggregated measurement. build_layer2b first aggregates measurements per category, but the MODE branch emits F.first(cat_col, ignorenulls=True) without ordering or comparing those aggregates. For categories A=1 and B=100, it can return A, and shuffle order can change the result.

Categorical values and field names are pasted into generated Python source without escaping. A value containing a double quote breaks the script, and a crafted value (for example one returned by a `domain_resolver` that reads distinct values from the facts table) can inject arbitrary Python into the script the user then runs on the cluster. `build_layer2a` builds `f'(F.col("{cat_field.name}") == "{cat_val}")'` and `f'...alias("{alias}")'` with plain f-string interpolation. `PivotedColumn.__init__` only checks values for the `__` separator (`_check_name_part`). docs/general_plan.md (Plan 09) says domain values may come from `SELECT DISTINCT` on the data. A value like `A"), __import__("os").system("..."), F.lit("` still parses as valid Python and would run. The same unescaped `f'"{c}"'` pattern is used for id, time and measurement names in every build_* method. Only table names use `!r`.

Categorical values containing quotation marks produce invalid generated Python. Pivot predicates interpolate cat_val directly inside double quotes, and aliases are interpolated similarly. Substituting the valid string value a"b into a pivot combination causes ast.parse(build_layer2a(...).code) to raise SyntaxError; CategoricalField performs no escaping or restriction on allowed_values.

The Plan 16 criterion "All transformations are lazy until the returned callable is invoked" is not met. The generator returns a plain script string with no callable, and each step runs an eager `saveAsTable` action, while the class docstring says everything is lazy. docs/general_plan.md Plan 16 says the final output is "a `PySparkOutput` containing a callable that, when invoked with a `SparkSession`, executes the full pipeline", and its acceptance criterion requires laziness until that call. Every build_* method instead emits `...write.mode('overwrite').saveAsTable(...)` (lines 78, 127, 211, 286, 388). That is a Spark action that runs immediately and overwrites tables. `generate` returns `PySparkOutput(code=full_code)`, a string. The docstring at line 36 says "All generated transformations are lazy". The script also uses an undefined global `spark` instead of taking a session as a parameter.

Different source and target time granularities are ignored, producing features at the wrong temporal resolution. TimeField explicitly supports source_granularity, target_granularity and truncation_required, but build_layer2a groups by the original time column directly. build_mob_table and build_layer2b likewise use raw timestamps. With daily source data and a monthly target, two dates in one month remain separate periods and temporal windows count daily rows.

Several distinct temporal operators are emitted with identical expressions. PROM_P is the same as PROM_U, SUM_P the same as SUM_U, XM the same as FREQ, and RATIO is just a windowed SUM. The feature table may therefore contain duplicate columns under names that suggest different features, and nobody has signed off what these operators mean. `_temporal_pyspark_expr`: the PROM_P branch returns the same `F.avg(...).over(frame_w)` as PROM_U. SUM_P matches SUM_U. The XM branch is a copy of FREQ. RATIO returns `F.sum({col_ref}).over({frame_w})`, which is not a ratio. No spec or code in the repo defines these operators differently, so the builder's reading is an unrecorded assumption.

When there are no Layer 3 features (or no Layer 2A columns), the generated code is a syntax error, because the template always adds a trailing comma line after the list it joins. `build_layer3` emits `'    "mob",
' + f"{feat_list},
" + ")"`. With `pipeline.layer3` empty, `feat_list` is `""`, so the output contains a line holding only `,`, which is invalid Python. `build_layer2a` has the same issue with `f"{agg_list},
"` (line 125). `build_final_join` does guard on `pipeline.layer3`, but `build_layer3` does not. An empty layer3 can happen through `operators_override`.

The tests check only that the generated text parses and contains certain keywords. They never run the code against a Spark or mocked session and never check computed values, so they cannot catch the broken ENTROPY expression or the wrong MODE logic. Every assertion is `_is_valid_python(...)` (ast.parse) or a substring check such as `"crossJoin" in self._code()` or `"features" in code`. `test_empty_layer2b_returns_comment` (line 278) asserts `"layer2b" not in out.code or "no distributional" in out.code`, which accepts almost any output. Plan 16 allows a mocked SparkSession, but none is used.

The generator tests do not verify executable Spark behavior or calculated feature values. The distributional and temporal tests check keyword presence and ast.parse success; test_all_metrics_valid_python accepts expressions with invalid Spark API calls, including the ENTROPY expression. No test executes the generated transformations against a Spark session or checks expected metric values.

The `generate()` override weakens the public interface. It declares return type `object` instead of `FeatureStoreOutput`, and its type checks use `assert`, which is stripped under `python -O`. `def generate(self, pipeline: FeatureStorePipeline) -> object:` followed by `assert isinstance(result, FeatureStoreOutput)` and `assert isinstance(result.code, _PS)`. It also re-imports `PySparkOutput` as `_PS` even though the module already imports it at the top.

The change contains dead or misleading code: a conditional whose two branches are identical, an unused helper, and an unused import in the generated header. `col_ref = (f'F.col("{src_col}")' if not isinstance(feat.source, DistributionalColumn) else f'F.col("{src_col}")')` has the same value on both branches. `_spark_read` (line 51) is never called. `_HEADER` imports `SparkSession`, but the generated script never uses it and relies on a global `spark`.
